q: Between the capillaries and the cells is a watery liquid called tissue fluid.
e: Tissue fluid acts as the immediate environment for cellular exchange.

q: Most of the water from tissue fluid reenters capillaries by osmosis.
e: The low water potential inside the capillary draws fluid back in at the venule end.

q: Some fluid passes into the nervous system to be transported back to the blood.
e: Excess fluid passes into the lymphatic system to be transported back to the blood.

q: The lymphatic system transports the fluid, called lymph, back to the blood by opening into the subclavian veins.
e: The thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct drain lymph into the subclavian veins.

q: The lacteals that carry fats from villi of the small intestine are part of the lymphatic system.
e: Lacteals absorb lipid-soluble nutrients that are too large to enter blood capillaries directly.

q: Before lymph passes back into the blood, it is filtered to remove dead cells and bacteria in lymph nodes.
e: Lymph nodes contain immune cells that trap and destroy pathogens before the fluid reenters circulation.
